title: Advanced Leadership
tagline: Move from leading a team to leading leaders, functions and change, with judgement, influence and integrity.
description:
Most managers are promoted for being good at the work. The step to senior leadership asks for something different: you now lead people who lead others, you decide with incomplete information, you need support from colleagues you do not control, and the culture of your function starts to look like you.

**Advanced Leadership** is built for that step. Over five sessions you will work on how you lead yourself under pressure, how you think and decide strategically, how you build teams of managers who own results, how you lead change and win support without formal authority, and how you set a culture that performs ethically and lasts beyond you.

Every idea is applied to realistic situations from Pakistani organisations: a bank rolling out a new core system, a telecom restructuring its regions, an FMCG business entering new cities, a family-owned group professionalising its management. Each session ends with a scored test, and the certification closes with a demanding, timed final exam built on scenarios where more than one answer looks reasonable. Passing it shows that you can apply senior leadership judgement, not just recall theory.
audience: Mid-level and senior managers who already lead teams and now lead other managers or a whole function
Newly promoted heads of department, regional heads and general managers
High-potential leaders in succession pools preparing for wider responsibility
Project and transformation leads who must drive change across functions they do not control
Founders and family members professionalising the management of a growing business
outcomes: Lead yourself deliberately: know your values and triggers, regulate emotion under pressure and show steady executive presence
Frame strategic problems, choose the right decision approach for the level of uncertainty and guard against common biases
Build teams of managers with real trust and accountability, delegate at scale and coach leaders to grow
Plan and lead change by mapping stakeholders, building coalitions and working with resistance rather than against it
Influence peers, seniors and partners without relying on positional authority
Shape an ethical, high-performing culture, handle difficult conversations well and build resilience and succession

quest.name: The Karakoram Ascent
quest.premise: You have been chosen to lead an expedition up an unclimbed Karakoram peak. The mountain will not reward strength alone: the higher you climb, the more you depend on judgement, on rope teams that trust each other, and on porters, partners and officials you cannot order about. From Base Camp to the Summit Ridge, each stage tests a different side of senior leadership. Reach the top, pass the final ascent, and earn your place among those who lead leaders.

badge.name: Summit Leader
badge.description: Awarded for completing The Karakoram Ascent and passing the Advanced Leadership final exam: proven judgement in leading leaders, change and culture.

sessions.title: Leading Yourself: Identity, Values and Presence
sessions.summary: Before you lead leaders, you lead yourself. Redefine what your job now is, clarify the values you lead by, manage your emotions and triggers under pressure, see your blind spots and build an executive presence based on substance.
objectives: Explain how the job changes when you move from leading a team to leading leaders or a function
Turn personal values into clear operating principles and use them in hard trade-offs
Apply the four areas of emotional intelligence to manage triggers and pressure
Use structured feedback to uncover blind spots that grow with seniority
Show executive presence through composure, clarity and concise communication

cards.title: The transition nobody trains you for
cards.body:
Each step up the leadership ladder changes three things at once: the **skills** you need, how you spend your **time**, and what you **value** about work. Many senior leaders fail not because they lack ability, but because they keep doing the job they were good at one level down.

| Moving from | To leading leaders or a function |
|---|---|
| Solving problems yourself | Building managers who solve them |
| Measured on your team's output | Measured on a system of teams and its results |
| Deep in one specialism | Balancing functions you never worked in |
| Short planning horizon (weeks) | Longer horizon (quarters and years) |
| Valuing being the expert | Valuing other people's success |

Three warning signs that you have not made the shift:

- **You are the bottleneck.** Decisions queue at your desk, and your managers wait for you rather than decide.
- **You skip levels by habit.** You go straight to the frontline and fix things, which quietly undermines the managers in between.
- **Your calendar looks like your old job.** Most of your week is operational detail, and almost none of it is direction, people or cross-functional work.

The hardest part is the value shift. It feels unproductive at first to spend an afternoon coaching a branch manager instead of closing the problem yourself in twenty minutes. But at this level, your real output is the capability of the people below you. If you fix it yourself, you solve one problem; if you build a manager who can fix it, you solve the next hundred.

cards.title: From personal values to operating principles
cards.body:
Values only help a leader when they are specific enough to guide a decision. 'Integrity' or 'excellence' on a wall poster does not tell anyone what to do when a top client asks for an exception. Senior leaders turn values into **operating principles**: short statements of how they will behave, especially when it costs something.

A simple way to build them:

1. **Recall peak and low moments.** When were you proudest of how you led? When did you feel you let yourself down? The values hide in those stories.
2. **Name 3 to 5 core values.** Fewer is better; a long list cannot guide choices.
3. **Write each as a behaviour.** For example, 'Fairness' becomes 'I decide promotions on evidence I could show to the person who was not chosen.'
4. **Test against a real dilemma.** If the principle does not change what you would do, it is too vague.
5. **Share them.** When your team knows your principles, they can predict your decisions and act without asking.

**Values conflict with each other.** Loyalty to an old colleague can pull against fairness to the team. Speed can pull against thoroughness. Mature leaders do not pretend these tensions away; they decide which value takes priority in which situation, and explain why.

In many Pakistani organisations, pressure arrives through relationships: a call from a senior's relative, a request from a long-standing distributor, an expectation of loyalty to the person who promoted you. Clear operating principles, stated early and applied consistently, protect you. People stop asking for exceptions when they learn that your answer does not depend on who is asking.

cards.title: Ayesha's first quarter as regional head
cards.body:
Ayesha Siddiqui was the best branch manager in her bank's Lahore network. When she was promoted to regional head over 28 branches and four area managers, she kept her old habits. Every credit exception above PKR 2 million came to her personally. She visited branches unannounced and reworked their sales plans on the spot. Branch staff loved her energy.

By the end of her first quarter, the picture was worrying. Turnaround time for exceptions had grown from two days to six, because files waited for her. Two of her four area managers had stopped making decisions at all; one told HR, 'Why should I decide when she will change it anyway?' Her own manager asked why the regional plan for the next year was late.

Ayesha took two weeks to reset:

- She wrote a one-page **decision guide**: area managers would approve exceptions up to PKR 5 million within clear criteria, and she would review a sample each month rather than every file.
- She stopped unannounced fixes. When she visited a branch, she went **with** the area manager and coached them afterwards in private.
- She blocked two half-days a week for planning and for meetings with heads of operations, risk and marketing.

Three months later, turnaround was back under two days, the area managers were visibly more confident, and the regional plan was praised for its cross-functional thinking. Ayesha admitted the hardest part was emotional: 'I had to accept that my value was no longer in the files I touched.'

cards.question: Which sign most clearly shows that a newly promoted head of function has NOT yet made the transition to leading leaders?
options: They spend time each week with peers from other functions
Decisions routinely wait for their personal approval
They hold regular one-to-ones with their direct-report managers
Their calendar includes protected time for planning
cards.explanation: When decisions queue for the leader, they have become the bottleneck and their managers are not deciding. The other options are signs of a healthy transition: peer work, coaching managers and time for direction.

cards.title: Emotional intelligence at senior level
cards.body:
Emotional intelligence (EI) is the ability to recognise and manage emotions in yourself and others. It is commonly described in four areas:

| Area | Inward or outward | What it looks like for a senior leader |
|---|---|---|
| **Self-awareness** | Inward | Knowing your moods, triggers, strengths and limits as they happen |
| **Self-management** | Inward | Staying composed, adaptable and positive under pressure; not acting on every impulse |
| **Social awareness** | Outward | Reading the room, sensing unspoken concerns, understanding the politics of a group |
| **Relationship management** | Outward | Influencing, resolving conflict, coaching and building networks |

The areas build on each other. You cannot manage what you have not noticed, and you cannot read others well while flooded by your own emotion.

**Why it matters more as you rise.** Your emotional state spreads. When a team member is irritable, a few people notice; when a regional head is irritable, the whole region adjusts its behaviour. People hide bad news, delay escalation and tell you what you want to hear. Leaders are often the last to learn that their mood is setting the tone.

**The hijack.** Under threat, the brain's fast alarm system can trigger a fight-or-flight reaction before the reasoning part catches up. A sharp remark in a board meeting or a public challenge from a peer can provoke a response you regret within seconds. The practical defence is to **create a gap** between trigger and response: a slow breath, a question before an answer ('Help me understand what you mean'), or an agreed pause ('Let me come back to you on that by tomorrow').

cards.title: Keep a trigger log for two weeks
cards.body:
For two working weeks, note each moment you felt a strong negative reaction at work. Record: **what happened**, **what you felt** (name the emotion precisely: embarrassed, disrespected, anxious, not just 'angry'), **what you did**, and **what you wish you had done**.

Most leaders find two or three repeating patterns, for example being challenged in front of seniors, or a team missing a deadline they promised. Once you know your patterns, plan a default response for each in advance. A planned response is far easier to use under pressure than willpower.

**Common mistake:** confusing suppression with self-management. Swallowing anger and then sending a cold email at midnight is not regulation. Regulation means you notice the emotion, choose a response, and deal with the issue at a time and place you pick.

cards.title: Blind spots grow with seniority
cards.body:
The **Johari window** is a simple model of self-knowledge with four panes: what is known to you and to others (**open**), known to others but not to you (**blind**), known to you but hidden from others (**hidden**), and unknown to everyone (**unknown**). Growth comes from enlarging the open pane: asking for feedback shrinks the blind area, and appropriate self-disclosure shrinks the hidden one.

The uncomfortable truth is that the blind pane tends to **grow** as you are promoted. Three forces cause this:

- **Power filters information.** People soften or hold back feedback to someone who controls their bonus and career.
- **Hierarchical norms.** In cultures with high respect for seniority, including many Pakistani workplaces, openly correcting a senior can feel improper, so feedback goes sideways to colleagues instead of up to you.
- **Success reinforces habits.** The behaviours that got you promoted feel proven, even when they no longer fit the role.

Practical ways to see your blind spots:

1. **Structured 360-degree feedback** with anonymous input from managers, peers and reports, ideally debriefed with a coach.
2. **Ask specific, future-focused questions.** 'What is one thing I could do differently in our weekly reviews to make them more useful?' is easier to answer honestly than 'Any feedback for me?'
3. **Reward the first honest answer.** How you react to the first piece of candid feedback decides whether you will ever get a second. Thank the person, do not defend, and show visible action.
4. **Find a truth-teller.** A trusted peer or mentor outside your reporting line who will tell you what others will not.

cards.question: A divisional head says, 'My team is very open with me; nobody has raised any concerns in our meetings this year.' What is the most likely explanation an experienced coach would explore first?
options: The team genuinely has no concerns worth raising
The meetings are too long for concerns to come up
The team lacks the technical knowledge to spot problems
Power and hierarchy are filtering what people are willing to say
cards.explanation: Silence from a team is rarely proof of openness. Power differences and respect for hierarchy commonly filter what reaches senior leaders, so a coach would test whether concerns are going unspoken. The other explanations are possible but less likely and would not be the first hypothesis.

cards.title: Kamran's outburst and the repair
cards.body:
Kamran Qureshi, general manager for a telecom operator's southern region, opened his monthly review in Karachi with bad news: network complaints in Hyderabad had doubled. When the Hyderabad zonal manager, Sana Baloch, began explaining a vendor delay, Kamran cut her off in front of twelve colleagues: 'I don't want stories, I want results.' The room went quiet. For the rest of the meeting, no one raised a single risk.

That evening, Kamran reflected on what he had lost. The vendor delay was real information he needed; by shutting Sana down publicly, he had taught everyone that bad news is punished. He also recognised his trigger: he felt exposed because his own director had questioned him about Hyderabad that morning.

His repair had three parts:

- **Private apology the next morning.** He told Sana directly that cutting her off was wrong, and asked her to walk him through the vendor issue. He did not add 'but' to the apology.
- **Public acknowledgement.** At the next review, he told the group: 'Last month I shut down an important explanation. I want to hear risks early, even when the news is bad.'
- **A changed routine.** He moved a 'risks and blockers' slot to the start of every review, before performance numbers, and asked one manager each month to present the biggest risk in their zone.

Within two months, issues were being raised a week or two earlier than before. Kamran's lesson: one public reaction can undo months of saying 'my door is open', and the repair must be at least as visible as the damage.

cards.title: Executive presence is substance, shown well
cards.body:
Executive presence is the quality that makes others trust your judgement and want to follow your lead, especially in senior rooms. It is often mistaken for confidence, polish or a loud voice. In practice it rests on three pillars:

- **Composure.** You stay steady when things go wrong. In a crisis, people watch the leader's face before they listen to the words. Calm, measured responses signal that the situation is under control.
- **Clarity.** You can state the issue, your view and what you need in a few sentences. Senior audiences have little time and many priorities.
- **Credibility.** Your view is grounded in evidence, you know the numbers, you admit what you do not know, and you do what you said you would do.

Appearance and manner matter only as far as they help or distract from these. Dressing appropriately for the setting, making eye contact and speaking without filler words remove noise, but no amount of polish replaces substance.

**Presence in hierarchical settings.** In many Pakistani boardrooms, juniors defer to seniors and contradiction is expressed indirectly. Presence here does not mean challenging everyone bluntly. It means stating your view respectfully but unambiguously ('My recommendation is not to proceed until the audit is complete, for two reasons'), holding it when pushed back on without becoming defensive, and changing it only when given a better argument, not simply because a more senior person disagrees.

**Presence in writing.** At senior levels, much of your presence travels through emails and papers. Lead with the conclusion, keep it short, and make the decision you need from the reader obvious.

cards.title: Brief like a senior: conclusion first
cards.body:
When updating senior leaders, use a three-part structure:

1. **Bottom line:** the conclusion or decision you need, in one sentence. ('I recommend we delay the Peshawar launch by six weeks.')
2. **Why:** the two or three most important reasons, with one key number each.
3. **What next:** the risks, what you need from them, and by when.

**Common mistake:** telling the story in the order it happened. Senior listeners lose patience waiting for the point, and may interrupt before you reach your recommendation. Put the conclusion first, then offer detail if they ask for it.

cards.title: Managing your energy and attention
cards.body:
At senior levels, time stops being the scarcest resource; **attention** is. Your calendar fills with meetings others schedule, your inbox sets your priorities, and the important but not urgent work (strategy, talent, relationships) is crowded out by the urgent.

Three practices help:

- **Audit your calendar.** Take the last four weeks and sort each hour into: direction and strategy, people and talent, cross-functional and external relationships, operational detail, and administration. Compare this with what your role actually needs. Many new senior leaders discover that over half their time goes to operational detail their managers should own.
- **Protect thinking time.** Block regular, uninterrupted time for planning and reflection, and treat it as seriously as a meeting with your own manager. Strategy rarely happens in the gaps between meetings.
- **Manage energy, not just hours.** Schedule demanding work, such as difficult conversations or key decisions, at times when you are fresh. Notice what drains and restores you. Long hours with poor sleep reduce judgement measurably, and senior errors are expensive.

**Role modelling.** Your team copies your working patterns. If you send messages at 1 a.m. and expect quick replies, you set an always-on norm, even if you say you value balance. If you must work late, schedule messages for the morning. What you do speaks louder than what you say.

cards.question: Which statement best describes executive presence as taught in this session?
options: A confident, polished personal style that impresses senior audiences
Composure, clarity and credibility, with style only supporting substance
The ability to dominate discussions and win arguments in senior meetings
Formal dress and manner that signal respect for hierarchy
cards.explanation: Executive presence rests on composure, clarity and credibility. Style and appearance only matter insofar as they support or distract from substance. Dominating discussions or relying on polish alone undermine trust over time.

cards.title: Base Camp take-aways
items: Promotion to leading leaders changes your skills, your use of time and what you value: your output is now other people's capability.
Values guide decisions only when written as specific operating principles and applied consistently, regardless of who is asking.
Emotional intelligence builds from self-awareness to self-management, then social awareness and relationship management.
Create a gap between trigger and response; regulation is choosing a response, not suppressing emotion.
Blind spots grow with power; seek specific feedback and reward the first honest answer.
Executive presence is composure, clarity and credibility; lead with your conclusion.

cards.prompt: Look at your calendar for the last two weeks. What share of your time went to work your managers should own? Write down one decision type you will formally hand over this month, and one operating principle you want your team to be able to predict from you.

quiz.question: Bilal has just been promoted from area sales manager to national sales head of an FMCG company, leading five regional managers. Which change in how he spends his time best reflects a successful transition?
options: Joining more distributor visits so he stays close to the market
Reviewing every regional manager's weekly route plans for accuracy
Moving time to direction, coaching his managers and peer work
Personally handling key accounts so regional managers can focus on volume
quiz.explanation: Leading leaders means spending time on direction, building managers' capability and cross-functional relationships. Market visits have value, but making them his main focus, checking route plans or taking key accounts away from his managers keeps him in his old job and weakens his regional managers.

quiz.question: Which version of a value is most useful as an operating principle for a senior leader?
options: I make promotion decisions on evidence I could show to the candidates not selected
I believe in fairness and treat all team members equally at all times
Fairness is one of our core values and guides everything we do
I aim to be a fair, honest and transparent leader in every situation, whatever the pressure
quiz.explanation: An operating principle is specific enough to change a decision. Only the first option describes a concrete behaviour that can be tested. The others restate the value in general terms and would not guide a hard choice.

quiz.question: In a quarterly review, a peer challenges Farah's numbers in front of the CEO. She feels her face go hot and wants to point out the peer's own missed targets. According to this session, what is the best immediate move?
options: Answer firmly by pointing out the peer's targets so the CEO sees a balanced picture
Stay silent for the rest of the meeting and raise a complaint with HR afterwards
Agree with the challenge to avoid conflict and correct the numbers later by email
Pause, ask the peer to clarify the specific concern, then respond on the facts
quiz.explanation: Creating a gap between trigger and response, for example by asking a clarifying question, lets reasoning catch up and keeps the discussion on facts. Counter-attacking escalates the hijack, while silence or false agreement is suppression rather than regulation.

quiz.question: In the four-area model of emotional intelligence, why is self-awareness usually treated as the foundation?
options: It is the area most valued by boards when they assess senior leaders
You cannot manage emotions you have not first noticed
It can be measured more reliably than the other three areas
It is the only area that cannot be developed through coaching
quiz.explanation: The areas build on each other: noticing your own emotions makes self-management possible and frees attention to read others. The other options are not reasons given for its foundational role, and self-awareness can certainly be developed.

quiz.question: Which statement about the Johari window and seniority is most accurate?
options: The hidden area shrinks automatically as leaders gain authority
The blind area tends to grow because power filters candid feedback
The unknown area disappears once a leader completes a 360 review
The open area grows naturally as people respect a leader's position
quiz.explanation: As leaders rise, people become more cautious about telling them uncomfortable truths, so the blind area tends to grow unless the leader actively seeks feedback. The other statements are not supported: none of these changes happens automatically.

quiz.question: Usman, a new plant head in Faisalabad, asks his managers, 'Any feedback for me?' at the end of every meeting and always hears 'No, sir, all good.' What change is most likely to produce useful feedback?
options: Announce that giving upward feedback is now mandatory and will be part of appraisals
Stop asking, since the managers have clearly said things are fine
Bring in an external consultant to observe meetings for a month
Ask a specific, forward-looking question and respond without defending
quiz.explanation: Specific, forward-looking questions are easier to answer honestly, and how the leader reacts to the first candid answer decides whether more follow. Making feedback mandatory adds pressure without safety; stopping accepts the filter; an observer may help but does not open the channel with his managers.

quiz.question: Rabia, head of compliance at a bank, must brief the managing director in a five-minute slot on whether to pause a new digital account product. Which opening is strongest?
options: I recommend pausing the launch for four weeks until two KYC control gaps are closed
Let me take you through how our review unfolded over the last month
There are several issues we have found that I would like to discuss
Before I give a view, it is important that you understand the full regulatory background
quiz.explanation: Senior briefings should lead with the bottom line and the decision needed, then give reasons. Narrating the review, listing issues without a view, or starting with background risks losing the listener before the recommendation is heard.

quiz.question: After publicly snapping at a zonal manager, a regional head wants to repair the damage. Which approach best fits the guidance in this session?
options: Apologise privately and leave it there, so the incident is not reopened in front of the whole team
Say nothing, and show warmth to the manager over the following weeks instead
Apologise privately, acknowledge it publicly and change a routine to invite risks early
Apologise publicly, while explaining the pressure he was under from his director
quiz.explanation: Public damage needs a repair at least as visible as the harm, plus a structural change so people see it will not recur. A private apology alone leaves the group's lesson ('bad news is punished') in place, silence fixes nothing, and an apology padded with excuses weakens it.

quiz.question: Zainab, a newly appointed head of HR, audits her last four weeks and finds 60% of her time went on approving routine leave exceptions and resolving individual payroll queries. What should she do first?
options: Work longer hours for a few months so she can add strategic work on top of current tasks
Ask her assistant to filter her emails so she only sees urgent items
Accept it, since responsive service builds credibility with the business
Define which decisions her managers will own and redirect queries to them
quiz.explanation: The audit shows she is doing work her managers should own. Handing over decision rights frees attention for strategic people work and builds her team. Longer hours are unsustainable, email filtering does not move the decisions, and accepting the pattern keeps her in the wrong job.

quiz.question: In a board meeting, a senior director dismisses Omer's recommendation to delay an acquisition. Omer believes the due diligence is incomplete. What does executive presence look like here?
options: Withdraw the recommendation, since openly disagreeing with a senior director in a board meeting is unwise
Restate the recommendation calmly with the key evidence, and stay open to better arguments
Escalate immediately to the chairperson to overrule the director
Raise his voice slightly to show conviction and keep the floor
quiz.explanation: Presence in hierarchical settings means stating a view respectfully but clearly, holding it when pushed back on, and changing it only for a better argument, not for seniority. Withdrawing abandons a reasoned view, escalating publicly damages trust, and raising his voice replaces substance with force.

sessions.title: Strategic Thinking and Decisions Under Uncertainty
sessions.summary: Senior leaders are paid to make the calls others cannot. Learn to frame the real problem, match your decision approach to the level of uncertainty, use scenarios and expected value, catch the biases that distort judgement and make trade-offs with clear decision rights.
objectives: Describe strategy as a set of explicit choices, including what not to do
Frame a problem precisely before solving it, using issue trees and testable hypotheses
Choose a decision approach that fits clear, complicated, complex or chaotic situations
Use scenarios, expected value and reversibility to decide under uncertainty
Recognise and reduce common cognitive biases and clarify who decides

cards.title: Strategy is a set of choices
cards.body:
Many documents called 'strategy' are really lists of goals ('become the market leader') or activities ('launch three products'). Strategy is different: it is a coherent set of **choices** about where to compete and how to win, made in the face of limited resources and real competition.

Useful questions for any function or business unit:

- **Where will we play?** Which customers, regions, products or channels will we focus on, and which will we deliberately not serve?
- **How will we win there?** What will make customers choose us over the alternatives: cost, quality, speed, relationships, convenience?
- **What capabilities must we build?** What do we need to be excellent at, and what can we partner for or outsource?
- **What will we stop?** If nothing is being stopped, you have probably not made a real choice.

**Thinking in systems.** Strategic thinkers look beyond the first effect of a decision to the second and third. Cutting the field force in Sindh saves cost this year (first effect); distributors receive fewer visits and start favouring a competitor (second effect); shelf share falls and next year's revenue drops by more than the cost saved (third effect). Before deciding, ask: **and then what?**

**Zooming out and in.** Senior leaders must move between the long view (where is the industry heading in five years?) and the operational detail that proves whether a strategy is working (are we actually winning the target customers this quarter?). Staying only at the top produces strategies nobody can execute; staying only in detail produces busy teams heading nowhere in particular.

cards.title: Frame the problem before you solve it
cards.body:
The most expensive mistake in senior decision-making is solving the wrong problem well. Before analysing options, spend time on the **question itself**.

**1. State the problem as a specific question.** 'Sales are down' is a symptom. 'Why have repeat orders from Tier-2 city retailers fallen 18% since March, and what can we do to recover them by year-end?' is a question you can work on.

**2. Break it down with an issue tree.** Split the question into parts that do not overlap and together cover the whole problem. For falling repeat orders, the branches might be: fewer retailers ordering, smaller orders per retailer, or less frequent orders. Each branch splits further until you reach things you can test with data.

**3. Form hypotheses early.** Rather than collecting all possible data, state your best current explanation ('Retailers are switching because a competitor offers 30-day credit') and look for evidence that would prove it **wrong**. This is faster and protects against only seeing what supports you.

**4. Ask 'what would have to be true?'** For each option, list the conditions that must hold for it to succeed. Then check which conditions are least certain and test those first. This turns an argument about opinions into a plan for gathering evidence.

**5. Separate the decision from the people.** In many organisations, proposals are judged by who presents them. A clear problem statement and agreed criteria make it easier to judge ideas on merit, which matters especially when a junior analyst's view contradicts a senior manager's.

cards.title: Reframing the northern expansion
cards.body:
A Lahore-based snacks company had grown strongly in Punjab. The board asked the commercial director, Hira Memon, to 'expand into Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and Balochistan'. The sales team had already proposed opening depots in Peshawar and Quetta and hiring 40 order bookers, at a first-year cost of around PKR 180 million.

Hira first reframed the question. Instead of 'How do we expand north and west?' she asked: **'Which new markets can deliver profitable growth of PKR 1 billion in revenue within three years, given our production capacity and brand strength?'** This made it clear that KP and Balochistan were options, not givens.

She built an issue tree: market size and growth, competitive intensity, route-to-market cost, product fit and capacity. For each market she listed what would have to be true for success, including: retailers would stock a new Punjab brand without heavy credit; local distributors would partner on reasonable margins; transport costs would stay below 6% of sales.

Testing these assumptions cheaply changed the plan. A three-month pilot with one Peshawar distributor showed strong retailer acceptance, but Quetta's transport and credit costs were nearly double the assumption. Meanwhile, analysis showed that southern Punjab and interior Sindh, already reachable from existing depots, offered faster growth at lower cost.

The final strategy: expand through distributors in Peshawar and southern Punjab, postpone Quetta, and use the savings to add a second production shift. The board accepted it because the reasoning was transparent, and because Hira had shown what they were choosing **not** to do and why.

cards.question: A head of retail banking says, 'Our problem is that deposits are down.' What is the best next step in framing the problem?
options: Launch a deposit campaign immediately to reverse the trend
Turn the symptom into a specific question and break it into testable parts
Ask each branch manager to submit ideas for growing deposits
Benchmark deposit rates against the three largest competitors
cards.explanation: Framing comes before solving: a specific question broken into non-overlapping parts shows where the decline actually comes from. Campaigns, idea collection and benchmarking may all follow, but without framing they risk addressing the wrong cause.

cards.title: Match the approach to the situation
cards.body:
Not every decision should be made the same way. The **Cynefin** framework, developed by Dave Snowden, helps leaders diagnose what kind of situation they are in:

| Domain | Cause and effect | Best approach | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Clear** | Obvious to anyone | Sense, categorise, respond: apply best practice | Processing a standard account-opening request |
| **Complicated** | Knowable with expert analysis | Sense, analyse, respond: use experts, compare options | Choosing between two ERP vendors |
| **Complex** | Only clear in hindsight; patterns emerge | Probe, sense, respond: run safe-to-fail experiments | Changing a sales culture or launching into a new consumer segment |
| **Chaotic** | No visible relationship; crisis | Act, sense, respond: stabilise first, then assess | A cyber attack takes down payment channels |

A fifth state, **confusion** (earlier called disorder), is when you do not know which domain applies; the risk is that each person defaults to their favourite approach.

**Common leadership errors:**

- Treating a **complex** problem as complicated: commissioning a long study to find the 'right answer' when only experimentation will reveal what works.
- Treating a **chaotic** situation as complicated: holding analysis meetings while the crisis spreads.
- Treating a **clear** situation as complex: running pilots for something that has a known best practice.
- **Complacency in the clear domain:** rigidly following rules after conditions have changed, which can push a situation suddenly into chaos.

In complex situations, leaders should design several small, low-cost experiments, watch what emerges, amplify what works and dampen what does not.

cards.title: Tools for deciding under uncertainty
cards.body:
**Scenario planning.** Instead of a single forecast, describe two to four plausible futures based on the most important and most uncertain drivers, such as exchange-rate movement and the pace of digital adoption. Then ask: which choices perform acceptably across most scenarios (**robust**), and which bet heavily on one future? Agree **signposts**, early indicators that tell you which scenario is unfolding.

**Expected value.** For options with uncertain outcomes, multiply each outcome by its probability and add them up. Option A: 60% chance of PKR 50 million profit and 40% chance of PKR 20 million loss gives 0.6 x 50 + 0.4 x (-20) = **PKR 22 million**. Expected value is a useful anchor, but it is not the whole answer: if a PKR 20 million loss would breach a covenant or threaten the business, a lower but safer option may be wiser. Consider your capacity to absorb the downside.

**Reversibility.** Ask whether a decision is a one-way door (hard or costly to undo, such as closing a plant or exiting a market) or a two-way door (easy to reverse, such as a pricing test in one city). One-way doors deserve careful analysis and senior involvement. Two-way doors should be made quickly and close to the work; over-analysing them wastes time and teaches the organisation to fear action.

**Keep options open.** Where uncertainty is high, prefer moves that buy learning cheaply: pilots, phased investments, partnerships with exit clauses. You pay a little for the right to decide later with better information.

cards.question: Payment channels at a mid-sized bank go down after a suspected cyber attack, and customers are complaining on social media. Using Cynefin, what should the leadership team do first?
options: Commission an expert review to analyse the root cause before taking action
Act immediately to stabilise and contain the situation, then assess and respond
Run several small experiments to see which recovery approach works best
Apply the standard incident checklist exactly and avoid any deviation
cards.explanation: This is a chaotic situation: the priority is to act to establish stability (contain, communicate), then sense and respond. Analysis first suits complicated problems, experiments suit complex ones, and rigid checklist use assumes a clear domain. The checklist may still help, but should not stop urgent judgement.

cards.title: The biases that distort senior judgement
cards.body:
Our minds use fast shortcuts that usually work well but fail in predictable ways, especially under pressure, with incomplete information or when we are emotionally invested. Seniority does not protect you; confidence and past success can make some biases stronger.

| Bias | What happens | Leadership example |
|---|---|---|
| **Confirmation bias** | We seek and believe evidence that supports what we already think | Asking the team to 'find data to support' a decision already made |
| **Anchoring** | The first number we hear shapes our estimate | Budget discussions stuck near last year's figure regardless of need |
| **Sunk cost** | We continue because of what we have already spent | Pouring more into a failing project 'because we have invested PKR 300 million' |
| **Overconfidence** | We overrate our accuracy and underrate risks | Plans with no margin for delay; ranges that are far too narrow |
| **Availability** | Recent or vivid events feel more likely | Over-investing in protection against last year's crisis |
| **Groupthink** | Desire for harmony suppresses dissent | Everyone agrees with the chairman; concerns surface only after failure |
| **Status quo bias** | We prefer the current state even when change is better | Keeping an old vendor because switching feels risky |

Groupthink is especially strong where hierarchy is respected and disagreement with a senior can feel disrespectful. A meeting in which nobody disagrees with the most senior person is a warning sign, not a success.

Knowing about biases is not enough to avoid them: we spot them much more easily in others than in ourselves. The defence is to build **processes** that counter them, which the next card covers.

cards.title: Build debiasing into the process
cards.body:
- **Pre-mortem.** Before committing, ask the team to imagine it is a year later and the decision has failed badly. Each person writes down why. This makes it safe to voice doubts and surfaces risks that optimism hides.
- **Agree criteria before seeing options.** Decide what matters (cost, risk, speed, fit) and how much, before proposals arrive, so you do not bend the criteria to fit a favourite.
- **Speak in reverse seniority.** Ask the most junior people to give their views first, so they are not anchored by the boss.
- **Rotate a challenger.** Assign someone to argue the strongest case against the preferred option; rotate the role so it is not personal.
- **Use base rates.** Ask how similar projects have gone, inside and outside the company, before trusting your own estimate.
- **Judge the decision separately from the outcome.** A good decision can have a bad result because of luck, and vice versa. Review the quality of the reasoning, not only what happened.

cards.title: The core banking project that would not stop
cards.body:
A Pakistani microfinance bank had spent PKR 420 million and two years on a new core banking system. The vendor kept missing milestones, and the latest estimate showed another 14 months and PKR 250 million to go live. In the steering committee, the chief operating officer, Tariq Mengal, argued: 'We have come too far to stop now.' Everyone nodded.

The new chief risk officer, Nadia Shah, asked for one session to be run differently. She opened with a simple question: **'If we had not spent anything yet, knowing what we know today, would we choose this vendor and this plan?'** This removed the sunk cost from the discussion. She then ran a pre-mortem: each member wrote privately why the project might still fail. The cards revealed concerns no one had raised in meetings: the vendor's local team had high turnover, two key modules had never been deployed in a microfinance setting, and the bank's own data migration was months behind.

The committee commissioned a four-week independent review against criteria agreed in advance: remaining cost, delivery risk, regulatory fit and exit cost. The review found that a phased approach, keeping the old system for lending while moving deposits to a proven cloud platform, would cost less and carry far lower risk.

The decision was painful; some of the PKR 420 million could not be recovered. But the money already spent was gone whatever they chose. The only question that mattered was which path gave the best result from **today** onwards.

cards.title: Trade-offs and decision rights
cards.body:
Strategic decisions involve real trade-offs: growth against risk, speed against quality, short-term profit against long-term capability. Good leaders make the trade-off **explicit** ('we are accepting a higher default rate in exchange for reaching new customers, within these limits') instead of pretending they can have everything.

**Clarify who decides.** Many decisions stall not because they are hard but because nobody knows who owns them. A role-based approach helps. For each important decision, name:

- who **recommends** (does the analysis and proposes),
- who must give **input** (consulted, but cannot block),
- who must **agree** (has a formal veto, such as legal or compliance; keep this list short),
- who **decides** (one person, accountable for the call),
- who will **carry out** the decision.

One decider is crucial. Committees that decide by unanimous agreement often produce delay or weak compromises.

**Disagree and commit.** Once a decision is made after genuine debate, everyone, including those who argued against it, commits to making it work. Leaders earn this by ensuring people were truly heard. Passive resistance after a decision, sometimes called 'yes in the meeting, no in the corridor', is far more damaging than open disagreement before it.

**Communicate the why.** For major trade-offs, explain what was considered, what was chosen and what was given up. People accept decisions they disagree with far more readily when they understand the reasoning.

cards.question: In a steering committee, a sponsor argues, 'We have already spent PKR 300 million on this project, so we must finish it.' Which question best counters the bias?
options: How much more would it cost to finish compared with what we have spent?
Who approved the original budget, and were they aware of these risks?
Knowing what we know now, would we start this project from scratch today?
Could we recover any of the PKR 300 million if we stopped now?
cards.explanation: Sunk cost bias is countered by judging the choice from today forward. Asking whether you would start it today removes the money already spent from the reasoning. Comparing with past spend keeps the sunk cost in view; blame does not help the decision; recoverable value is relevant but secondary.

cards.title: Keep a decision journal
cards.body:
For important decisions, write a short note at the time: the question, the options considered, what you expected to happen and how confident you were, and what you decided. Review it six to twelve months later.

Without a record, memory rewrites history: we remember being more certain about the outcomes that happened. A journal shows you your real accuracy, which biases you lean towards, and whether your confidence matches your track record. It also helps you explain decisions to boards and auditors later.

cards.title: Camp I take-aways
items: Strategy is explicit choices about where to play and how to win, including what you will stop.
Frame the problem as a specific question, break it into testable parts and ask what would have to be true.
Match the approach to the domain: best practice when clear, analysis when complicated, experiments when complex, immediate action when chaotic.
Use scenarios, expected value and reversibility; move fast on two-way doors and carefully on one-way doors.
Biases are countered by process: pre-mortems, criteria first, reverse seniority, challengers and base rates.
Name one decider, make trade-offs explicit and expect disagree-and-commit once people are genuinely heard.

cards.prompt: Think of a major decision currently on your desk. Which Cynefin domain is it really in, and is your approach matching it? Write down what would have to be true for your preferred option to succeed, and which of those conditions you are least sure of.

quiz.question: A telecom's head of strategy presents a plan titled 'Strategy 2028' with three goals: grow revenue 15% a year, be the most loved brand and lead in 5G. What is the most important thing missing?
options: A detailed financial model showing year-by-year revenue projections
Explicit choices about where to compete, how to win and what to stop
A comparison of the plan with the strategies of global telecom operators
A communication campaign to build employee excitement about the goals
quiz.explanation: Goals are not strategy. Without choices about where to play, how to win and what not to do, the plan gives no guidance on resource allocation. A financial model, benchmarks and communication may all help, but none supplies the missing choices.

quiz.question: A pharma company cuts its medical representatives in interior Sindh by 30% to save PKR 60 million. Doctors receive fewer visits, prescriptions shift to a competitor, and next year revenue in the region falls by PKR 110 million. Which thinking habit would most likely have prevented this?
options: Benchmarking field-force size against competitors in the same region
Using expected value to calculate the most likely savings
Applying best practice from the company's Punjab operations
Tracing second- and third-order effects before deciding
quiz.explanation: The loss came from consequences beyond the first effect. Asking 'and then what?' would have exposed the link between fewer visits, lost prescriptions and lower revenue. Benchmarking and expected value of savings do not capture the chain, and copying Punjab practice ignores local conditions.

quiz.question: Which problem statement is best framed for senior decision-making?
options: Why has our share of salary accounts from new corporate clients in Karachi fallen from 22% to 15% this year, and how can we regain 20% by June?
We need to improve our performance in salary accounts across the country
Our corporate banking team is not working hard enough on new clients
Competitors are taking our customers and we must respond quickly
quiz.explanation: A well-framed problem is specific, measurable, bounded in scope and time, and does not assume the cause. The others are vague, blame a cause without evidence, or describe a reaction rather than a question.

quiz.question: A retail chain wants to change its store staff culture from 'stock keepers' to 'customer advisers'. Nobody in the company has done this before and staff reactions are hard to predict. Which approach best fits?
options: Hire a consultant to design the definitive programme, then roll it out to all stores
Apply the training programme used successfully by another retailer, unchanged
Run several small, safe-to-fail pilots in different stores and scale what works
Issue clear new standard operating procedures and audit compliance monthly
quiz.explanation: Culture change with unpredictable reactions is a complex problem, where cause and effect are clear only in hindsight. Probe-sense-respond through small experiments is the right approach. The others treat it as complicated or clear, assuming the answer can be designed or copied in advance.

quiz.question: Option A has a 70% chance of earning PKR 40 million and a 30% chance of losing PKR 30 million. Option B earns a certain PKR 15 million. What is the expected value of Option A, and what else should the leader consider?
options: PKR 19 million; whether the business could absorb a PKR 30 million loss
PKR 28 million; whether the 70% probability is reliable
PKR 10 million; whether Option B's return is truly certain
PKR 19 million; nothing else matters, since Option A clearly beats Option B on expected value
quiz.explanation: 0.7 x 40 + 0.3 x (-30) = 28 - 9 = PKR 19 million, above B's 15 million. But expected value is not the whole answer: the leader must consider the capacity to absorb the downside. The PKR 28 million figure ignores the loss, and saying nothing else matters ignores risk.

quiz.question: Which decision is best treated as a two-way door that should be made quickly and close to the work?
options: Closing the company's only plant in Hyderabad and moving production to Lahore
Signing a ten-year exclusive distribution contract with heavy exit penalties
Testing a new price point for one product in Multan for six weeks
Selling a business unit to a competitor
quiz.explanation: A limited pricing test in one city is easy and cheap to reverse, so it should be decided quickly by the people closest to it. Plant closure, long exclusive contracts with penalties and divestment are costly or impossible to undo and deserve careful senior analysis.

quiz.question: In a budget meeting, the CFO opens with, 'Last year we spent PKR 85 million on marketing.' The team's proposals all land between PKR 80 and 95 million, although the new strategy needs a very different mix. Which bias is most clearly at work, and what is the best fix?
options: Confirmation bias; ask the team to look for evidence against their proposals
Groupthink; appoint a devil's advocate for future budget meetings
Availability bias; review marketing campaigns from several years, not just the most recent one
Anchoring; build the budget from the strategy's needs before showing last year's figure
quiz.explanation: Estimates clustering around the first number heard is anchoring. The fix is to build the budget from needs before the anchor appears. The other biases may exist, but they do not explain the clustering, and their fixes would not remove the anchor.

quiz.question: Before approving a major market entry, the managing director asks the team to imagine that, one year later, it has failed badly, and to write down why. What is the main purpose of this technique?
options: To lower the team's expectations so they are not disappointed later
To make it safe to voice doubts and surface risks optimism hides
To calculate the probability of failure more precisely
To prepare the explanation the board will need if the project fails
quiz.explanation: A pre-mortem legitimises doubt and surfaces risks that people would not raise in an optimistic planning meeting. It is not about lowering expectations, does not produce precise probabilities, and is not mainly about preparing excuses.

quiz.question: A family-owned textile group has decisions stalling for months because five directors must all agree on any capital spend above PKR 10 million. What change would most improve decision speed without losing important input?
options: Name one accountable decider per decision type, keep veto rights to a few, and consult others
Raise the approval threshold to PKR 50 million so that fewer decisions need all five directors to agree
Require all five directors to meet weekly so decisions are made faster
Let the chairman override any director who has not responded within a month
quiz.explanation: Clarifying decision roles, with one decider, a short list of those who must agree, and others giving input, removes the unanimity trap while keeping input. Raising the threshold only moves the problem, weekly meetings keep unanimity, and a one-month override still allows long delays.

quiz.question: After a well-reasoned decision to enter a new segment, an unexpected currency shock causes a loss. In the review, the board wants to blame the decision-makers. What is the most appropriate leadership response?
options: Accept the blame, since a loss proves the decision was wrong
Argue that losses after careful analysis are always due to bad luck, so no review is needed
Focus the review only on finding which forecast was most wrong
Review the quality of the reasoning and information separately from the outcome
quiz.explanation: Good decisions can produce bad outcomes through events outside anyone's control. Judging reasoning separately from results allows real learning, for instance about whether currency risk was considered. Accepting blame automatically or denying any review both skip that learning, and focusing only on forecasts is too narrow.

sessions.title: Building High-Performing Teams and Leading Leaders
sessions.summary: On the high ice, every climber is roped to others. Turn a group of capable managers into a real leadership team: build trust and psychological safety, hold people accountable without blame, delegate outcomes at scale and coach leaders to grow.
objectives: Distinguish a real leadership team from a group of managers who report to the same person
Build trust and psychological safety and explain why they improve performance
Create accountability through clear commitments and follow-through, without blame
Delegate outcomes and decision rights matched to each manager's readiness
Coach leaders using structured conversations and behaviour-based feedback

cards.title: A team, or a group with the same boss?
cards.body:
Many senior leaders say they have a 'leadership team' when what they really have is a **hub and spoke**: each manager deals with the boss one-to-one about their own area, and the weekly meeting is a round of individual updates. Nobody owns the whole.

A real leadership team has:

- **A shared purpose and collective goals** that no member can achieve alone, for example reducing end-to-end loan turnaround, which needs sales, credit and operations together.
- **Clear membership and interdependence.** Members know who is on the team and need each other to succeed.
- **An enabling structure**: the right size (often five to nine), clear norms about how decisions are made and how disagreement is handled, and meetings designed for joint work rather than reporting.
- **A supportive context**: information, resources and rewards that reinforce collective success. If every bonus depends only on individual targets, expect individual behaviour.
- **Coaching from the leader** at the right moments: at launch, at the midpoint, and when reviewing what was learned.

Research on teams consistently suggests that these conditions, set up well at the start, explain more of a team's performance than the leader's personal style during meetings.

**The 'first team' idea.** Senior managers tend to see the team they lead as their first loyalty. For a leadership team to work, members must also treat their peer group as a first team, putting the success of the whole function ahead of defending their own area. Leaders build this by setting shared goals, rewarding collaboration and calling out turf protection when it appears.

cards.title: Trust and psychological safety
cards.body:
**Trust** is the willingness to be vulnerable to someone else's actions. A useful way to break it down is the **trust equation** popularised by David Maister and colleagues:

**Trust = (Credibility + Reliability + Intimacy) / Self-orientation**

- **Credibility:** do you know what you are talking about, and are you honest about what you do not know?
- **Reliability:** do you do what you say, consistently?
- **Intimacy:** do people feel safe sharing difficult things with you?
- **Self-orientation:** are you focused on yourself (your image, your bonus, winning the argument) or on others? Because it sits below the line, high self-orientation damages trust more than anything else.

**Psychological safety**, a concept developed by Amy Edmondson, is a shared belief in a team that it is safe to take interpersonal risks: to ask a question, admit a mistake, raise a concern or challenge an idea without being embarrassed or punished. Edmondson's early hospital research found that better-led teams **reported more** errors, not because they made more mistakes, but because people felt safe to speak up, which allowed problems to be caught and fixed.

Psychological safety is **not** about being nice or lowering standards. The highest-performing teams combine high safety with high standards. Low safety with high standards creates anxiety and hidden problems; high safety with low standards creates comfort without results.

Leaders build safety by framing work as a learning problem ('we have not done this before, so we will need everyone's eyes'), admitting their own mistakes, asking genuine questions, and responding to bad news with appreciation and action rather than blame.

cards.title: From updates to a real team
cards.body:
Asma Durrani became general manager of a pharmaceutical company's commercial division, leading the heads of sales, marketing, medical affairs, supply planning and key accounts. Her predecessor had run a Monday meeting where each head spent fifteen minutes presenting numbers. Problems between functions were handled privately with the GM.

The symptoms were familiar: marketing blamed supply for stock-outs during campaigns; sales blamed marketing for unrealistic launch plans; supply blamed sales for poor forecasts. Each head was hitting most of their own targets while the division missed its overall growth goal.

Asma made four changes over six months:

1. **Shared goals.** She agreed three division-level goals with the team, including forecast accuracy and on-shelf availability for the top 20 products, and made them 40% of every head's bonus.
2. **Redesigned meetings.** Numbers were shared in writing beforehand. Meeting time went to two or three cross-functional problems, each owned by a pair of heads.
3. **Explicit norms.** The team agreed how they would work: disagree in the room, not after; no surprises; decisions recorded with one owner.
4. **Her own behaviour.** When stock-outs hit a key antibiotic, she opened the discussion by naming her own error in pushing a launch date, which made it easier for others to admit theirs.

Within a year, forecast accuracy improved from about 60% to 78%, and the heads began resolving issues among themselves before they reached her. As her head of supply said: 'We stopped reporting to Asma and started working with each other.'

cards.question: According to the trust equation, which change would most improve a leader's trustworthiness if their credibility and reliability are already high?
options: Increasing the number of meetings they hold with the team
Showing more technical expertise in reviews
Reducing their focus on their own image and interests
Making more promises to demonstrate commitment
cards.explanation: Self-orientation is the denominator in the trust equation, so lowering it raises trust most. More meetings do not necessarily build trust, more expertise adds to credibility that is already high, and more promises only help if kept.

cards.title: Accountability without blame
cards.body:
Accountability means people own outcomes and answer for them, both success and failure. In weak cultures, accountability is either absent (nobody follows up) or confused with **blame** (finding someone to punish when things go wrong). Neither produces performance.

Real accountability rests on four elements:

1. **Clear expectations.** What exactly is the outcome, by when, and what does good look like? Many 'accountability problems' are really clarity problems.
2. **Explicit commitment.** The person agrees to the goal and the plan, ideally in their own words. Imposed targets are owned less than agreed ones.
3. **Regular, predictable follow-through.** Progress is reviewed on a rhythm everyone knows. Leaders who forget what was agreed teach their teams that commitments are optional.
4. **Consistent consequences.** Recognition when commitments are met; a direct, private conversation when they are not; and, if the pattern continues, formal consequences, applied the same way whoever the person is.

**Peer accountability** is the mark of a mature leadership team. Members challenge each other ('You committed to sharing the forecast by Thursday; it came on Monday and our plan slipped') without waiting for the boss. Leaders encourage this by not being the only one who ever holds others to account.

**Avoid rescuing.** When a manager is struggling, it is tempting to take the problem back. Doing this occasionally in a crisis is fine; doing it routinely teaches the manager that deadlines will be met by someone else.

In relationship-based cultures, holding a long-serving colleague or a well-connected manager to account can feel awkward. Inconsistency is quickly noticed, however, and destroys the credibility of every standard you set.

cards.title: Delegation at scale
cards.body:
When you lead managers, you cannot delegate tasks one by one; you must delegate **outcomes and decision rights**. 'Prepare the branch staffing plan' is a task. 'Own staffing across the northern region so that service levels stay above 90% within the approved budget' is an outcome with authority attached.

**Levels of delegated authority.** Make the level explicit for each area:

| Level | What the manager does |
|---|---|
| 1. Inform | Gathers facts; you decide |
| 2. Recommend | Proposes a decision; you approve |
| 3. Decide and tell | Decides, then informs you |
| 4. Decide | Decides and acts; you review periodically |
| 5. Full ownership | Owns the area, including setting its goals |

Most delegation failures come from mismatched assumptions: the manager thinks they are at level 3, the leader expected level 2.

**Match the level to readiness.** Readiness combines **competence** (skill and experience in this specific area) and **commitment** (confidence and motivation). A strong manager new to a task needs more direction for that task, even if highly capable elsewhere. A skilled but discouraged manager needs support and encouragement more than instructions. Situational approaches to leadership make exactly this point: the same person may need a different style for different tasks.

**Agree the guardrails.** Effective delegation states the outcome, the authority level, the boundaries (budget, policies, non-negotiables), the resources, and how and when you will check in. Then step back. Checking in too often signals distrust; never checking in signals abandonment.

cards.title: Write a one-page delegation agreement
cards.body:
For any significant area you hand over, agree on one page:

- **Outcome:** what success looks like, in measurable terms.
- **Authority level:** which decisions they make alone, which they recommend.
- **Boundaries:** budget limits, policies and anything that must be escalated.
- **Support:** people, data and access you will provide.
- **Check-ins:** when and how you will review progress, and what would trigger an earlier conversation.

**Common mistake:** delegating the work but not the authority. If a manager must still ask you for every spending decision, you have delegated responsibility without power, which demotivates capable people fast.

cards.question: Saad, an experienced and confident finance controller, has just been asked to lead a budget process for the first time in a new business unit. What delegation approach best fits?
options: Full ownership immediately, given his seniority and confidence
More direction and closer check-ins for this specific task at first
No delegation until he has observed someone else do it for a year
Minimal contact, so he does not feel his competence is questioned
cards.explanation: Readiness is task-specific. Saad is committed but new to this task, so he needs more direction and checking at first, with authority growing as he shows competence. Full ownership or minimal contact ignores his lack of experience here, and waiting a year wastes his ability.

cards.title: Coaching leaders to grow
cards.body:
Coaching is helping someone think through their own situation and find their own way forward. It differs from **mentoring** (sharing your experience and advice) and **directing** (telling someone what to do). All three have their place. Directing suits a crisis or a true beginner; coaching suits capable people facing problems they can solve with better thinking, which describes most of your direct-report managers.

A widely used structure is **GROW**:

- **Goal:** What do you want to achieve from this conversation, and in the situation itself?
- **Reality:** What is happening now? What have you tried? What is getting in the way?
- **Options:** What could you do? What else? What would you do if there were no constraints?
- **Way forward (or Will):** What will you do, by when? How committed are you, on a scale of 1 to 10? What support do you need?

**Good coaching questions** are open, short and about the other person's thinking: 'What is the real challenge here for you?' 'What would you advise a peer in the same position?' Poor questions are advice in disguise: 'Have you thought about calling the distributor?'

The hardest discipline is **resisting the urge to fix**. Senior leaders usually see a solution quickly. Giving it may solve today's issue but teaches the manager to bring every problem back. Asking one more question, and tolerating a short silence, often produces a better answer that the manager actually owns.

Coaching does not mean you never give your view. A good pattern is to ask first, then offer your perspective if it adds something: 'Can I share one more angle to consider?'

cards.title: Faisal's struggling territory
cards.body:
Faisal Gill, an area manager for a mobile financial services company in southern Punjab, was missing his agent-acquisition target for the third month. His regional head, Mehwish Abbasi, had been telling him what to do in each review. Nothing had changed. She decided to coach instead, using GROW.

**Goal.** 'What would you like to get out of the next 30 minutes?' Faisal said he wanted a plan he believed in for the next quarter.

**Reality.** Mehwish asked what was really happening. After some hesitation, Faisal said the problem was not the number of agent visits but that newly signed shopkeepers stopped transacting within weeks because they ran out of e-float and could not rebalance easily. 'I have not said this before because the target is about sign-ups, not activity.'

**Options.** She asked what he could do. He listed three ideas; when asked 'What else?', he added a fourth: pairing new agents with nearby super-agents who could supply liquidity. Mehwish asked, 'Can I add one thought?' and suggested involving the liquidity team at head office.

**Way forward.** Faisal committed to piloting the pairing idea with 30 agents in Bahawalpur within two weeks, and rated his commitment 8 out of 10. When asked what would make it 10, he said permission to count active agents, not just sign-ups, in his pilot. Mehwish agreed to take that to her director.

The pilot raised 90-day agent activity sharply. More importantly, the coaching surfaced a flaw in the target itself that months of instructions had hidden.

cards.title: Give feedback as situation, behaviour, impact
cards.body:
Feedback lands better when it is specific and free of judgements about character. Describe the **situation** (when and where), the **behaviour** (what the person actually said or did, as a camera would record it), and the **impact** (the effect on you, the team or results). Then ask for their view.

Example: 'In yesterday's review with the risk team (situation), you interrupted their head three times before she finished (behaviour). She stopped contributing, and we left without her input on the credit limits (impact). How did you see it?'

**Common mistake:** labelling instead of describing. 'You were rude' invites defence; a description of behaviour invites discussion.

cards.title: Leading through other managers
cards.body:
Leading leaders brings challenges that do not exist when you lead individual contributors.

**Skip-level contact, done right.** Meeting people two levels down is valuable: you hear how strategy lands, spot talent and show you care. But it can easily undermine your managers. Good practice: tell managers about skip-level meetings and their purpose; listen and learn rather than give instructions; send issues back through the manager rather than solving them directly; and never use skip-levels to gather evidence against a manager without telling them.

**Do not reverse your managers' decisions casually.** If you overturn a manager's decision in front of their team, you tell everyone that the real authority sits with you, and people will start bypassing the manager. If a decision must change, discuss it privately and, where possible, let the manager announce the change.

**Leading former peers.** Promotion over colleagues is common in Pakistani organisations, where people often grow up together in the same company. Acknowledge the change openly, meet each former peer one-to-one to discuss expectations, and be consistent from day one: favouritism towards old friends, or harshness to prove you are not biased, both damage trust.

**Underperforming managers.** A weak manager hurts many people below them, so the cost of delay is multiplied. Diagnose first (clarity, skill, will, fit or circumstances), give clear expectations and support, set a defined time for improvement, and act if it does not come. Moving a struggling manager sideways without addressing the issue simply relocates the problem.

cards.question: During a skip-level meeting, a branch officer complains to the regional head that her area manager has refused her leave request unfairly. What should the regional head do?
options: Approve the leave on the spot to show the regional head listens
Promise to investigate the area manager's behaviour privately
Thank her, explore the concern, and raise it with the area manager to resolve
Tell her that leave matters should never be raised in skip-level meetings
cards.explanation: Listening respectfully and routing the issue back through the manager preserves the manager's authority while taking the concern seriously. Approving on the spot undermines the manager, a secret investigation damages trust, and dismissing the concern discourages honest input.

cards.title: Camp II take-aways
items: A real leadership team has shared goals, interdependence, clear norms and rewards that reinforce collective success.
Trust rises with credibility, reliability and intimacy, and falls sharply with self-orientation.
Psychological safety plus high standards drives performance; safety is not lowering the bar.
Accountability needs clear expectations, commitment, predictable follow-through and consistent consequences, not blame.
Delegate outcomes and decision rights, make the authority level explicit and match it to task-specific readiness.
Coach with GROW, resist the urge to fix, and route skip-level issues back through your managers.

cards.prompt: Is your management team a real team or a hub and spoke? Name one shared goal that would require your managers to depend on each other, and one area where you are still rescuing a manager instead of holding them accountable.

quiz.question: A head of operations runs a weekly meeting where each of six managers presents their own numbers and then leaves. Cross-functional problems are solved one-to-one with the head. What best describes this group?
options: A high-performing team that uses meeting time efficiently and avoids unnecessary debate
A self-managing team with strong peer accountability
A real team that simply needs shorter meetings
A hub-and-spoke group rather than a real leadership team
quiz.explanation: When members deal only with the leader and meetings are individual updates, there is no shared ownership or interdependence. It is a hub-and-spoke group. Efficiency, self-management or meeting length are not the issue; the missing element is collective work.

quiz.question: Edmondson's research found that better-led hospital teams reported more medication errors. What is the best explanation?
options: Better-led teams took on more complex and critically ill patients, so they made more errors
People felt safer to report mistakes, so more errors were surfaced and fixed
Better-led teams were stricter and punished errors more often
Weaker teams had better systems that prevented errors
quiz.explanation: The finding was explained by psychological safety: in well-led teams people were willing to report errors, so reported numbers were higher. The other options misread the research; punishment would reduce reporting, not increase it.

quiz.question: A divisional head says, 'My team feels very safe; we never pressure anyone and targets are flexible.' Performance is flat. Which description fits best?
options: Low safety with high standards, creating anxiety
High safety with high standards, the ideal combination for sustained performance
High safety with low standards, creating comfort without results
Low safety with low standards, creating apathy
quiz.explanation: Safety without demanding standards leads to comfort rather than performance. Psychological safety is meant to be combined with high standards, not to replace them. The other combinations do not match a team that feels safe but is not stretched.

quiz.question: Junaid, a zonal head, says his managers are 'not accountable'. On investigation, targets change most weeks, he rarely reviews agreed actions, and only some managers face consequences for missed deadlines. What is the most fundamental issue to fix first?
options: Junaid's own lack of clear expectations, follow-through and consistency
The managers' poor attitude, which needs formal warnings
The bonus scheme, which is not generous enough to motivate
The managers' lack of technical skill in planning, which needs a structured training programme
quiz.explanation: Accountability depends on clear expectations, predictable follow-through and consistent consequences, all of which are missing on Junaid's side. Warnings, bonus changes or training would not fix the system he has created.

quiz.question: A CFO tells a finance manager, 'Handle the audit preparation.' Later she is angry that he agreed the audit timetable with the external auditors without consulting her. What is the most likely root cause?
options: The manager deliberately exceeded his authority
The external auditors pressured the manager
The authority level was never made explicit
The CFO should not have delegated audit preparation
quiz.explanation: Most delegation conflicts come from mismatched assumptions about authority. The manager believed he could decide; the CFO expected a recommendation. There is no evidence of deliberate overreach or pressure, and delegating audit preparation is reasonable when done clearly.

quiz.question: Kiran is a highly skilled HR business partner who has become discouraged after her last two proposals were rejected. She is now leading a new engagement project she has done successfully before. Which style is most appropriate?
options: Detailed direction, with close supervision of each step until her confidence returns
Supportive: listen, encourage and involve her, with little instruction
Full delegation with no contact until the project ends
Directive, with a firm deadline and penalties for delay
quiz.explanation: Kiran has high competence for this task but lower commitment because she is discouraged. She needs support and involvement rather than instruction. Direction would insult her skill; full hands-off delegation ignores her low confidence; pressure would deepen discouragement.

quiz.question: In a coaching conversation, a manager says, 'I can't get the warehouse team to follow the new picking process.' Which response best reflects good coaching?
options: Have you thought about putting a supervisor on each shift?
In my experience, the answer is to retrain them and then enforce the process strictly on every shift
Let me speak to the warehouse team myself and sort it out
What have you tried so far, and what do you think is getting in the way?
quiz.explanation: An open question about reality helps the manager think and own the solution. The first option is advice disguised as a question, the second is mentoring or directing, and the third rescues the manager and removes ownership.

quiz.question: Which piece of feedback best follows the situation-behaviour-impact approach?
options: In Tuesday's client meeting, you shared the draft pricing before it was approved, and the client now expects that rate. What was your thinking?
